item.title: Physiological Representation of Social Evaluation: Modeling Human Eye Movements, Pupillary, and Neuronal Responses to Faces.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Face-based social evaluations are ubiquitous and consequential, yet it remains unclear how these evaluations are represented in spontaneous physiological responses. Across four studies (222 participants: 142 females, 57 males, 23 unreported; 503 neurons), we used a data-driven modeling framework to examine how facial appearance shapes eye movements, pupillary responses, and neuronal activity during face viewing. We asked what these responses reveal about the underlying social evaluations. Pupillary responses and hippocampal firing during saccades were driven by facial variation associated with an integrated combination of valence and power evaluations; fixation duration on the eyes and hippocampal firing during fixations were more selectively tuned to threat-related evaluations; amygdalar firing primarily tracked approachability-related valence. A prospective validation study confirmed that novel faces synthesized along these modeled directions elicited the predicted physiological responses in new participants. We also found evidence of individual differences: social anxiety selectively heightened the sensitivity of pupillary responses to face evaluations. These findings suggest that distinct physiological responses across attention, autonomic arousal, and medial temporal lobe activity reflect distinct but related facets of face-based social evaluation.Significance Statement Everyday social decisions hinge on split-second impressions of unfamiliar faces. When we see a face, we instantly judge the person's likely intention (positive ↔ negative valence) and social influence (high ↔ low power). Across four complementary studies, we show that these evaluative processes are reflected in physiological responses to faces across overt attention, autonomic arousal, and subcortical neuronal firing. Different physiological systems reflected partially distinct but related facets of social-evaluative meaning, including integrated valence-and-power, threat-related, and approachability-related evaluation.

item.title: The human hippocampus supports auditory coding and multisensory integration.
item.description:
PLoS biology
The hippocampus receives convergent input from multiple sensory systems, yet in humans it has been studied almost exclusively through vision. Here we examine how the hippocampus contributes to sensory processing beyond the visual modality and to the multisensory integration of visual information with these other modalities. Participants were exposed to multiple repetitions of short naturalistic movie clips, each presented in four formats: auditory-only, visual-only, congruent audiovisual, and incongruent audiovisual (audio and video from different movies). Using high-resolution fMRI, we measured univariate activation and multivariate representations across the longitudinal axis and subfields of the human hippocampus. Whereas univariate analyses detected only visual responses across hippocampal subregions, with no activation for auditory stimuli and no benefit of congruent stimuli, multivariate analyses revealed robust representations of both auditory and visual scenes. The posterior hippocampus showed enhanced pattern similarity for congruent stimuli relative to unisensory stimuli, especially in the left hemisphere, demonstrating multisensory facilitation. The anterior hippocampus showed crossmodal decoding between auditory and visual versions of the same clip, driven by the right hemisphere, suggesting a more abstract representation. Finally, whole-brain searchlight analyses revealed parallel effects in cortical regions known to support multisensory integration. These findings advance understanding of auditory and multisensory coding in the human hippocampus, revealing specialization and lateralization along its longitudinal axis.

item.title: What can behavior tell us about neural dynamics?
item.description:
Trends in cognitive sciences
For decades, systems neuroscience treated behavior as an endpoint: a simplified output, such as a button press, lick, or saccade, used to isolate neural computations. Richer behavioral measurements have expanded this view by revealing neural dynamics hidden by simple outputs. Yet behavior is not a direct readout of brain activity, because similar behavioral outputs can arise from different neural mechanisms. Interpreting neural dynamics is therefore an inverse problem with no straightforward solution. Behavior can constrain this problem by exposing sensorimotor loops, narrowing plausible explanations for population activity, and formalizing neural-behavioral relationships in joint models. Together, these approaches position behavior as a principled constraint on interpreting neural dynamics and latent cognitive, affective, and computational states.

item.title: Training Interbrain Synchrony through Dyadic Neurofeedback Modulates Empathy-for-Pain.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Dyadic neurofeedback offers a socially grounded approach for modulating neural processes that unfold between interacting individuals. While recent work demonstrates that dyadic neurofeedback can enhance inter-brain synchrony during interaction, whether its effects extend beyond the trained dyad remains unclear. Here, we examined whether dyadic neurofeedback targeting inter-brain synchrony in the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) is associated with changes in empathy-for-pain toward unfamiliar social targets. One hundred and eighty-six participants, randomly assigned to dyads, completed three neurofeedback training sessions within one week. Feedback was contingent on real-time IFG inter-brain synchrony in the neurofeedback group or on prerecorded signals in the sham-feedback control group. Empathy-for-pain was assessed before and after training. IFG inter-brain synchrony increased significantly across sessions in the neurofeedback group but not in the control group. Empathy-for-pain ratings showed different trajectories across conditions in the primary raw-data analysis, decreasing significantly in the sham-feedback group while remaining relatively stable in the neurofeedback group. A secondary analysis adjusting for a previously observed task-specific test-retest decline showed a significant increase in the neurofeedback group. Individuals with lower baseline trait empathy showed larger training-related increases in IFG inter-brain synchrony. Network analyses suggested broader changes involving IFG-IPL connectivity. Structural equation modeling further identified significant associations among training-related intra-brain synchrony, inter-brain synchrony, and empathy-for-pain change, consistent with the proposed relationship among these processes. Together, the findings indicate that dyadic neurofeedback can modulate IFG inter-brain synchrony across repeated training and may influence the trajectory of empathy-for-pain responding beyond the immediate training partner.

item.title: A Dynamic Model of Amygdala Circuits in Threat and Reward: Implications for Affective Disorders.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Animals must continuously evaluate their surroundings and select adaptive responses to survive in ever-changing environments. Central to this capacity is the assignment of importance to environmental cues, which guides motivated behavior toward rewarding opportunities and away from potential threats. Here we propose a theoretical framework, a dynamic motivational model based on threat and reward imminence, in which motivational states evolve continuously as a function of imminence rather than shifting between discrete stages. Within this framework, three interacting dimensions define the stimulus relevance of an environmental cue: salience, valence, and value. We leverage the amygdala as a substrate to illustrate the circuit mechanisms underlying importance assignment and examine how stimulus imminence drives motivational state transitions to promote adaptive behavior. Applied to affective disorders, it reframes amygdala dysfunction as projection- and circuit-specific stress adaptation rather than uniform regional hyperactivity, providing a common language for comparing major depressive disorder, anxiety disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder, and substance use disorders. By integrating animal circuit studies with human neuroimaging and clinical evidence, this framework positions amygdala-centered networks as candidate biomarkers for biologically informed subtyping and targets for personalized treatment in depression and related affective disorders.

item.title: Emotion knowledge is structured in a grid-like coordinate system in the human ventromedial prefrontal cortex.
item.description:
PLoS biology
Human emotional experiences vary widely in everyday life, yet they are systematically organized within a continuous affective space defined by valence and arousal. Although this circumplex organization has shaped decades of research, its neural implementation remains unclear. Here, we asked whether abstract emotion concepts are encoded using grid-like coordinate principles in the human brain. During fMRI, participants tracked trajectories through affective space conveyed through morphs of facial expressions and sequences of phrases. We found that ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) encoded affective space with robust hexadirectional modulation characteristic of grid-like coding. This coordinate representation generalized across stimulus modalities, indicating abstraction beyond perceptual features. The grid-like signal reflected a metric organization of emotion concepts independent of overt behavior, whereas distance-related signals in vmPFC predicted trial-by-trial affective judgements. Together, these findings suggest that emotion knowledge is structured by a grid-like coordinate system in the human brain that can support predictive inference and flexible decision-making.

item.title: Transcranial magnetic stimulation to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex modulates single-neuron activity in humans.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) is an established treatment for depression, yet the fundamental question of how cortical stimulation influences single neurons in deep brain circuits critical for mood regulation remains unanswered. Using a rare opportunity to record from intracranial microelectrodes while TMS was delivered in four neurosurgical patients, we evaluated the responses of 185 single neurons. Artifact cleaning enabled single-neuron spikes to be resolved as early as 8 ms after stimulation. We found that single-pulse TMS to the left dlPFC elicited time-locked firing responses in 46% of neurons (26% facilitated only, 19% suppressed only, 1% both). These responses occurred within deep bilateral cortical and subcortical structures, including the putamen and thalamus. Single-pulse TMS tended to facilitate spiking in striato-thalamic putative inhibitory neurons from ~8 ms, peaking at ~80 to 100 ms, and decaying until ~600 ms. In contrast, putative excitatory neurons and limbic areas were suppressed with a slower time course lasting to ~1,000 ms. TMS-evoked potentials recorded from intracranial depth macroelectrodes to quantify network activity revealed that the modulation of responsive neurons was positively correlated with cortico-striato-thalamic network activity and anticorrelated with limbic network activity in one participant with sufficient network and unit sampling. These results suggest that dlPFC TMS recruits a high percentage of neurons spanning cortical and subcortical brain regions bilaterally. The recruitment pattern selectively involves increasing the firing rate of inhibitory neurons in executive control networks while suppressing limbic excitatory drive, providing a candidate cellular mechanism for how cortical stimulation modulates distributed brain networks.

item.title: A causal account of the neural origins of mental fatigue.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Successful goal-directed behavior often requires the exertion of effortful cognitive control processes, but it remains unclear why engaging in cognitive control is experienced as effortful and induces fatigue. Here, we tested the hypothesis that sustained activation in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC)-a neural substrate of cognitive control-causally induces motivational fatigue via the accumulation of prefrontal glutamate metabolites. For this purpose, we combined brain stimulation with spectroscopy imaging to assess how increasing DLPFC excitability during an effortful mental task changes the motivation for mental effort and glutamate concentrations. We found that stimulating the DLPFC during mental effort exertion improved mental performance at the cost of increased posteffort motivational fatigue, suggesting a causal role of DLPFC activation for inducing fatigue. On the neural level, DLPFC activation during effortful cognition also increased prefrontal concentrations of glutamate, which statistically explained the fatigue-induced lower motivation for mental effort. A corresponding analysis of combined glutamate-glutamine (Glx) concentrations revealed converging effects. Together, these findings provide causal evidence that enhanced DLPFC activation contributes to fatigue via neurochemical changes, supporting neuro-metabolic accounts of fatigue and offering new insights into why demanding cognitive tasks are perceived as effortful.

item.title: State-Dependent EEG Markers of Excitation/Inhibition and Hemodynamic State Are Associated with Random Noise Stimulation Effects.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Background Non-invasive brain stimulation effects vary substantially across individuals, yet the physiological factors associated with this variability remain unclear. Objective We tested whether baseline and task-related EEG markers of excitation/inhibition (E/I) and hemodynamic state are associated with the effects of transcranial random noise stimulation (tRNS) on learning. Methods Participants completed a mathematical learning task during active or sham tRNS. We indexed E/I-related population dynamics using the EEG aperiodic exponent, for which lower values have been linked to relatively greater excitation than inhibition, and assessed hemodynamic state using fNIRS-derived oxygenated hemoglobin (HbO). Behavioral learning was modeled using generalized linear mixed-effects models. Results tRNS accelerated learning relative to sham stimulation but did not reliably induce pre-post changes in resting-state aperiodic exponent or HbO. Instead, stimulation effects were state-dependent. Higher resting-state aperiodic exponent and lower resting-state HbO were associated with greater behavioral gains under tRNS, while task-related aperiodic exponent was associated with stimulation-related differences in learning. Task-evoked HbO was associated with learning rate but did not significantly differentiate stimulation effects. Across modalities, the findings identify complementary electrophysiological and hemodynamic correlates of variability in learning under stimulation. However, statistical support for the EEG moderation effects was attenuated in models including participant-specific learning slopes, indicating sensitivity to random-effects specification and the need for replication. Conclusions The findings argue against a simple tonic-shift account of tRNS and support a state-dependent framework in which stimulation effects depend on ongoing electrophysiological and hemodynamic context. EEG and fNIRS provided complementary information about variability in learning and stimulation response, supporting multimodal approaches to understanding and individualizing neuromodulation.

item.title: Do autistic traits modulate the neural processing of logical rule violations in visual and auditory modalities?
item.description:
NeuroImage
Similarities in cognitive processing have been reported between individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and non-clinical individuals with autistic traits. However, previous research on autistic traits has primarily focused on social-emotional domains, with limited attention to abstract logical reasoning. Given that sensitivity to rules and patterns is a notable characteristic of the autism spectrum, logical rule processing may be particularly informative for understanding cognitive differences associated with autistic traits. The present research aimed to investigate the behavioral and neural responses of students with autistic traits to logical and illogical number sequences through two event-related potential studies. Based on Autism Spectrum Quotient-10 (AQ-10) scores, participants were categorized into High-AQ and Low-AQ groups. In Study 1, both groups judged whether visually presented logical and illogical three number sequences followed a logical incremental rule. In Study 2, both groups performed the same task as in Study 1, except number sequences were presented in the auditory modality. No significant group difference was found in response to logical number sequences in either study. However, relative to the Low-AQ group, the High-AQ group exhibited larger P2 and P3 amplitudes and more negative emotional reactions to illogical number sequences in the visual modality (Study 1), and more positive N1 and LPP amplitudes, and higher arousal ratings to illogical number sequences in the auditory modality (Study 2). These findings suggest that students with autistic traits may exhibit altered neural responses and heightened emotional reactivity specifically to stimuli that violate logical rules in separate visual and auditory studies.

item.title: Same Networks, Different Dynamics: Parsimony in Auditory Cognitive Task Processing.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Distinct cognitive states might be supported either by dedicated, task-specific brain networks or by flexible modulation within shared ones, a distinction central to understanding how the brain allocates neural resources. Guided by the principle of parsimony, we hypothesized that both language and numerical cognition, when matched for sensory modality and attentional demand, would engage a common network architecture differentiated primarily through targeted modulation of connectivity strength and temporal dynamics rather than wholesale reconfiguration. We applied a jackknife-based dynamic functional connectivity approach to examine time-varying network engagement during auditory language comprehension and auditory math problem-solving in 172 age- and sex-matched participants from the Human Connectome Project-Young Adult cohort, using the Desikan-Killiany atlas and an 85% participation threshold. Of the significant connections identified, many were retained across both tasks, with 87 connections common to story and math, compared with 26 story-associated and 11 math-associated connections. Rather than indicating a novel shared-core architecture, this overlap is consistent with prior evidence that task functional connectivity is strongly constrained by a common intrinsic connectivity backbone. We therefore used the shared edge set as a common network framework for testing how two modality-matched, but cognitively distinct auditory tasks differ in connectivity strength and temporal variability. Among the 87 shared connections, 84 showed significant task-related differences in mean connectivity strength, indicating that story-math differentiation was expressed primarily through quantitative modulation of shared connections rather than wholesale changes in edge membership. Exploratory rolling-correlation analyses further suggested that some edges may show temporal variability in math-story connectivity correspondence even when mean connectivity strength is similar, highlighting a potential dynamic feature not captured by static connectivity estimates alone. Together, these findings suggest that story and math processing rely on a broadly shared connectivity backbone, while task differentiation emerges through graded modulation of connection strength and, in some cases, temporal variability.

item.title: Integrating neuroplasticity into whole-brain modeling: From synapses to neural populations.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
The brain's ability to learn, adapt, and recover hinges on synaptic plasticity, yet most large-scale neural models overlook this core feature. In this review, we argue that embedding plasticity is essential for the simulation of realistic population-level brain activity. To this end, we explore specific computational attempts at scaling microscopic single-neuron plasticity rules to mesoscopic populations, drawing from mechanistic insights into short-term synaptic dynamics, long-term potentiation, and homeostatic regulation. We also discuss how plasticity mechanisms in neural field and neural mass models can potentially help us understand recovery trajectories, and how dysfunctional plasticity can play a role in them. Finally, we review state-of-the-art multiscale co-simulations methods that bridge spiking neuron networks with neural field and mass models and discuss their ability to link microscopic synaptic mechanisms with macroscopic brain dynamics. By embedding plasticity as a core feature, we can develop mean-field models that are more realistic and powerful tools for understanding brain function and recovery.

item.title: Capturing the Attentional Trade-off between Speech Planning and Comprehension.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
In conversation, future speakers often plan speech simultaneously with comprehension, which means that they must divide attentional resources between these processes. In this EEG study, we used responses to linguistic attention probes (i.e., syllable "BA" presented during spoken sentences) to track temporal variations in attention to comprehension. Participants were asked to listen to prerecorded sentences with expected or unexpected sentence-final words. Each sentence was presented twice, once with and once without the attention probe starting 100 msec after the target word onset. Participants saw a picture 50 msec before the target word. Depending on the test block (picture naming or button press), participants either named the picture or pressed the space bar, both after an 850-msec delay. The probes elicited a negative potential approximately 100 msec after probe onset (i.e., an attention probe effect) in all probe conditions. Unexpectedly, neither word expectancy nor speech planning influenced the timing or strength of the attention probe effect. This indicates that expectancy of words in Dutch does not affect the allocation of attention toward these words 100 msec after their onset (i.e., the time of the probe presentation). Interestingly, engaging in speech planning does not seem to divert attentional resources away from comprehension at the moment of probe presentation. These findings imply that listeners are able to effectively distribute their attentional resources between comprehension and speech planning and carry out these processes at the same time. Considering these unexpected findings, using attention probes might not be the best approach to capture variations in temporal attention in dual-task paradigms.

item.title: Theta and High-alpha Phase-locking Dynamics Unveil Face Perception in Ambiguous Stimuli.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Previous studies emphasize phase synchronization as a fundamental mechanism for integrating local features into coherent percepts. We employed a novel paradigm and dynamic graph analysis based on EEG to track neural dynamics associated with perceiving a face (or not) while keeping the stimuli identical. Thirty participants underwent a pretest to establish perceptual thresholds for detecting faces within images overlaid with visual noise. These thresholds were then applied in an EEG experiment with the same task, focusing on images with 50% and 75% detection probabilities. In the high-alpha band, we observed increased coupling (100-275 msec after stimulus onset) between the left and right occipitotemporal electrodes when an ambiguous stimulus was perceived as a face, indicating conscious face perception. The failure to perceive a face resulted in enhanced theta band phase synchronization between bilateral occipitotemporal electrodes and increased high-alpha-band coupling between the left frontal and right occipitotemporal electrodes, which showed face-selective responses. These synchronizations are likely to reflect the continuous gathering of individual bits of facial information rather than signaling the presence or absence of a face percept. Additionally, we identified frontal-occipitotemporal theta-band couplings related to the stimulus's informational content, irrespective of whether the inherent face was perceived. Our findings reveal distinct temporal dynamics in phase synchronization at specific frequencies, indicating a specialized system for face perception during integrated information processing across the frontal and visual cortex, resolving ambiguities.

item.title: Memory Traces Reflect How They Were Last Accessed.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Episodic memories are known to change with each act of retrieval. We hypothesize that accessing semantic knowledge in different ways during episodic retrieval-from unique perceptual features to taxonomic and thematic context-shapes how those memories are subsequently represented during recognition. In this fMRI study, human participants learned novel word-image pairs and underwent re-exposure that required accessing semantic knowledge at one of three different levels: item, category, or theme. Participants then completed a recognition task. Although behavioral memory performance was matched across conditions, neural activity during recognition varied based on prior semantic access history. Recognition patterns could be classified according to prior semantic access in early visual cortex, ventral temporal cortex, and the hippocampus for remembered concepts. A whole-brain searchlight analysis revealed bilateral clusters along the ventral visual stream where semantic access history was decodable. To further characterize how prior semantic access history shaped neural representations during recognition, we tested whether memories accessed at the same semantic level were expressed more similarly or distinctly in the brain. Category-level access increased similarity among items in early visual cortex, whereas item-level access led to more differentiated representations in the visual word form area. Together, these findings show that how we access semantic knowledge during episodic retrieval leaves measurable traces in subsequent neural representations, revealing how semantic-episodic interactions shape memory representations.

item.title: Intracranial Evidence for the Cerebellum's Role in Semantic Processing.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Language impairments in patients with cerebellar damage or dysfunction strongly implicate the cerebellum in language processing but the nature, timing, and specificity of its contributions are unclear. A clinical trial of cerebellar stimulation for motor recovery after middle cerebral artery stroke provided a rare opportunity to record invasive, intracranial local field potential activity from the cerebellar dentate nucleus of eight patients during language processing. Patients performed semantic priming tasks that either discouraged or encouraged semantic predictions. We found evidence for communication between the dentate nucleus and frontal scalp EEG sites in the alpha band when semantic predictions were violated. This did not occur when semantic predictions were fulfilled or when prediction violations were nonlinguistic in nature. This language-specific activity occurred in the N400 window where semantic processing of a visually presented word takes place. These data point to a linguistic feedback function that could help to account for the language deficits observed in diseases and disorders involving the cerebellum.

item.title: Neural Distinctions between Social and Nonsocial Reward Anticipation: An Examination of Activation Magnitude, Representational Patterns, Individual Differences, and Functional Connectivity.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Prevailing theories emphasize a "common neural currency" for social and nonsocial rewards, particularly during reward anticipation. However, direct comparisons of social and nonsocial reward anticipation remain limited, and clinical observations suggest that social reward processing can be selectively disrupted. The present fMRI study directly compared social and nonsocial reward anticipation to test differences in activation magnitude, functional connectivity, multivariate activity patterns, and modulation by individual differences in social reward motivation. Consistent with a "common neural currency" perspective, reward anticipation (collapsed across domains) was associated with increased activation in ventral striatum (VS), anterior insula (AI), dorsal ACC (DACC), and SMA. Furthermore, social reward anticipation did not significantly shape functional connectivity among ventral striatum, AI, DACC, and SMA. However, local activation patterns in AI and SMA reliably discriminated the anticipation of social versus monetary reward. Additional decoding emerged in TPJ, STS, and OFC-regions previously inconsistently linked to social reward anticipation or more commonly associated with later stages of reward processing. Moreover, individual differences in Need to Belong predicted greater ACC (including ventromedial PFC) engagement during social reward anticipation. These findings support the perspective that social and nonsocial reward anticipation share some neural circuitry but are dissociable when local activation patterns and social motivational priorities are considered. The current study recasts our understanding of ways in which social reward anticipation may be distinct and raises an expanded role for brain regions typically associated with reward and/or social processing.

item.title: Transformer Mechanisms Mimic Frontostriatal Gating Operations When Trained on Human Working Memory Tasks.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Working memory (WM) is thought to rely on sophisticated frontostriatal mechanisms for selective gating, supporting updating and readout of information to and from distinct memory "addresses" (neural populations). According to computational models, capacity limitations in WM arise due to challenges in "role addressability": learning to correctly bind items in memory to their respective roles and assigning credit to the corresponding gating operations. However, these conclusions are based on particular assumptions about biological neural networks, and it is unclear whether the principles generalize to other architectures. To address this question, we examine whether similar gating mechanisms emerge in Transformer neural network architectures, which have demonstrated success on tasks requiring executive function-the ability to represent, coordinate, and manage multiple subtasks-yet lack intentionally built-in gating mechanisms. We analyze the mechanisms that emerge within Transformers trained on human WM tasks explicitly designed to place demands on gating. We find that the Transformer's attention mechanism develops role-addressable input and output gating, but only when trained on task distributions that benefit from frontostriatal-like gating mechanisms. Moreover, these gating strategies support enhanced generalization and variable binding and increase the models' effective capacity to store and access multiple items in memory, resembling the constraints found in frontostriatal models. These results suggest that gating mechanisms serve a fundamental computational role in managing role addressability and binding and highlight opportunities for future research on computational similarities between modern artificial intelligence architectures and models of the human brain.

item.title: Slow Oscillations Modulate Overnight Brain Changes in Working Memory Function.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Working memory (WM), the transient storage and manipulation of information, is a cognitive function that can improve with training. Accumulating evidence suggests that sleep, particularly slow oscillations (SOs) that occur during nonrapid eye movement sleep, supports this improvement. Yet, how sleep and SOs in particular relate to neural processes supporting WM remains poorly understood. In this study, we investigated how WM-related neural activity evolves across nocturnal sleep and how these changes relate to neural processing during SOs. Participants performed a WM task during fMRI before and after sleep, with simultaneous EEG-fMRI capturing neural activity during the first 2.5 hr of sleep. Our results showed significant overnight changes in WM-related activity, characterized by reduced recruitment of the dorsal precuneus during WM encoding/maintenance phases and frontal regions during the retrieval phase of WM. In addition, sleep increased item-specific reinstatement in a sensory processing region during WM. This pattern of results suggests a combined influence of sleep on enhancing sensory reinstatement while reducing potential top-down control (i.e., reduced parietal and frontal activity). Critically, SO-related activity was directly linked to overnight activity changes: Stronger SO activation in the premotor cortex and ventromedial pFC predicted greater overnight reductions in WM-related activity, and multivoxel analyses in the ventral attention network revealed a parallel relationship. These findings suggest that SOs play a critical role in WM function by facilitating the reorganization of WM-related processing.

item.title: Exploring Neural Mechanisms Underlying Error-related Impairments in Active Working Memory Suggests an Adaptive Shielding of Contents during Cognitive Control.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Goal-directed behavior relies on cognitive flexibility-the ability to rapidly adapt ongoing thoughts and behaviors while preserving task-relevant information. The performance monitoring system optimizes such behavior by detecting and evaluating errors, whereas the working memory (WM) system maintains relevant information and protects it from interference. We previously showed that motor errors impaired active WM maintenance (Error-Related Impairment of Active working Memory [ERIAM]; [Wessel, J. R., Jiang, J., & Stolley, J. J. Action errors impair active working memory maintenance. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 151, 1325-1340, 2022]). Here, we investigated the source of ERIAM by tracking the contralateral delay activity (CDA), a neural marker of visual WM maintenance, throughout the error-making process. Forty-two participants maintained visual information in WM while performing a flanker task during the delay period. Consistent with prior results, a significant ERIAM effect occurred. We observed the canonical CDA before flanker task onset, and this CDA declined after the flanker task began. Following the flanker response, however, we observed a sustained contralateral positivity (CDAp). Critically, CDA amplitudes did not differ between motor correct and error trials before the flanker task, ruling out a general performance deficit. The CDA was also unaffected immediately after flanker onset, ruling out a perceptual interference explanation. Neural differences emerged only after the flanker response, supporting a genuinely error-related origin of the ERIAM effect. Importantly, CDAp was larger following correct responses than errors, and greater CDAp modulation predicted a smaller ERIAM effect. On the basis of prior work, we interpret CDAp as reflecting disengagement from WM storage, suggesting a possible adaptive shielding strategy. These findings provide clear evidence regarding the timing of the ERIAM effect and suggestive evidence regarding potential mechanisms underlying error-related interference in active WM maintenance. Future work will help determine the functional significance of CDAp and its relationship to WM storage and cognitive control.

item.title: Visual Perspective Shapes Subjective Experience: Dissociable Parietal Contributions to the Constructive Nature of Memory.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Subjective features of memory are often treated as secondary to the objective content of remembered events. However, growing evidence suggests that these features actively shape how memories are constructed, experienced, and used. Rather than treating visual perspective as a peripheral correlate of subjectivity, this review positions it as a key mechanism that shapes the memory. Because perspective can be flexibly controlled and reliably measured, it offers a unique window into how retrieval goals interact with mental simulation to produce vivid and emotionally resonant recollections. Drawing on behavioral and neuroimaging research, this review shows that visual perspective determines the spatial framing of memory and the emotional and sensory qualities of recollection. Focusing on the posterior parietal cortex, it outlines distinct roles for the angular gyrus (AG) and the precuneus in supporting perspective-dependent retrieval. The AG contributes to the selection and maintenance of a retrieval perspective, integrating perceptual and conceptual features into a coherent scene. In contrast, the precuneus supports spatial transformation and modulates the vividness, emotional tone, and embodied character of recollection, particularly when individuals recall events from a nondominant or shifted perspective. Together, these findings position visual perspective as a central mechanism in the construction of subjectivity. Understanding how perspective shapes the process of remembering provides insight into how memory supports emotion regulation, mental simulation, and the continuity of the self across time.

item.title: Investigation of the Prolonged Impact of Severe Socioeconomic Hardship and Mother's Perceived Social Support on Neurocognitive Development in Young Children in the Rural Ecuadorian Amazon.
item.description:
Developmental science
Children living in conditions of severe socioeconomic (SES) hardship are at elevated risk for neurocognitive delays, yet most developmental neuroscience research has focused on children in high-income, Western populations, limiting our understanding of diverse developmental contexts. This study examined maternal perceived social support as a potential buffer against the stressors associated with SES hardship on child neurocognitive development in a longitudinal sample of Indigenous families in the rural Ecuadorian Amazon. Twenty-eight children (M age = 28.02 months at T1; 57.6 months at T2) participated in the study completing an assessment of early cognitive ability at T1 and an inhibition task while functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) measured cortical activation at T2. A three-level linear mixed model revealed a significant interaction between early cognitive ability and maternal perceived social support on functional activation. Specifically, children of mothers with high social support showed no association between early cognitive ability and cortical activation, while those with low support exhibited atypical patterns (hyper- or hypoactivation), suggesting that increased maternal perceived social support may help buffer the risk exposure of chronic stressors associated with SES hardship. These findings underscore the importance of culturally embedded social resources in promoting resilience among children facing cumulative risk. Supporting maternal social networks may be a promising pathway for improving child neurodevelopment in underrepresented, low-resource communities and contributes to more inclusive global models of brain development.

item.title: Perceived Neighborhood Disadvantage Predicts Similarity in Amygdala Representations of Negative and Neutral Images in Early Adolescents.
item.description:
Developmental science
Neighborhood disadvantage encompasses multiple co-occurring adversities, including threat and deprivation, yet its underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear. Applying a dimensional framework to neighborhood contexts may help clarify how distinct features of disadvantage influence brain development. Here, we used representational similarity analysis to investigate associations between adolescents' neural representations of affective valence and neighborhood disadvantage, as measured by caregiver self-report and the Area Deprivation Index (ADI). One hundred and twenty-one adolescents aged 11 to 14 (Mage = 12.81 years old, 52.07% female, 28.93% White non-Hispanic) completed an emotional reactivity fMRI task. Caregiver-reported neighborhood disadvantage was associated with greater representational similarity in right amygdala between negative and neutral images, while no such effect emerged for the ADI. Follow-up analyses examined whether specific dimensions of disadvantage drove these effects. Although our measure did not map cleanly onto threat and deprivation dimensions, factor analyses revealed distinctions between social (e.g., crime, loitering) and physical (e.g., abandoned buildings, walkability) disadvantage-related items; our preliminary findings suggest that the effects of reported overall neighborhood disadvantage may be driven by characteristics of the social environment. No associations between caregiver-reported neighborhood disadvantage or ADI were observed for positive/neutral similarity. These findings provide preliminary evidence that neighborhood disadvantage may impact the amygdala's differentiation of negative and neutral stimuli during early adolescence, supporting the view that neighborhoods are a critical ecological context for development.

item.title: Early Emergence of Cultural Differences in Audiovisual Speech Perception.
item.description:
Developmental science
Integrating auditory and visual cues is a hallmark of human speech perception, yet adults from East Asian backgrounds show less reliance on visual speech than their Western counterparts. The origins of this cultural difference, however, remain unknown. To investigate whether this divergence is established early in infancy, we examined audiovisual integration in 6- to 12-month-old White Canadian (n = 111) and Chinese (n = 115) infants using a novel paradigm measuring their perception of the McGurk effect. Across four experiments, we found a clear developmental divergence: Canadian infants showed a stable McGurk effect from 6 months onward, whereas Chinese infants showed a more protracted developmental trajectory, a cultural pattern that was further highlighted when their integration was challenged by other-race faces. These findings provide the first direct evidence that cultural differences in multisensory speech perception are established within the first year of life, suggesting that the brain's strategy for binding sight and sound is shaped by early experience, with broad implications for theories of language acquisition and developmental science.

item.title: Nucleus Accumbens and Ventral Tegmental Area Functional Connectivity as a Marker of Reward Sensitivity in Infancy.
item.description:
Developmental science
Early functional connectivity within the brain's reward circuitry may provide insight into the developmental origins of individual differences in pleasure and motivation. This study examined resting-state functional connectivity between two key reward-related regions, the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and ventral tegmental area (VTA), in 94 one-month-old infants (58% male; M = 4.84 weeks, SD = 0.86) and its association with later reward-related temperament. Infants completed a resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging scan during natural sleep with a mean of 11.09 (SD = 2.78) min of retained low-motion data. Caregivers reported their infants' temperament at age six months, including high- and low-intensity pleasure as indicators of individual differences relevant to reward sensitivity. Positive resting-state functional connectivity between the NAc and VTA was present in early infancy (Cohen's d = 0.44, 95% CI [0.22, 0.65]), p < 0.001). Less positive NAc-VTA connectivity was associated with greater high-intensity pleasure at six months (β = -0.32, 95% CI [-0.54, -0.10], p = 0.004), indicating that infants with stronger connectivity between these regions exhibited less enjoyment of highly stimulating, energetic activities. NAc-VTA connectivity was not associated with low-intensity pleasure (β = -0.01, 95% CI [-0.24, 0.21], p = 0.908). These findings suggest that early variation in mesolimbic connectivity may serve as a marker of emerging individual differences in reward responsiveness, with implications for understanding affective development in infancy.

item.title: Hippocampal-prefrontal cortical interactions and neural representations of memory.
item.description:
Current biology : CB
The ability to store memories and access past experiences when making decisions in the present is fundamental to cognition. The hippocampus is critical for these processes and has been a primary site of investigation in the learning and memory field for the last several decades. However, it is also clear that the hippocampus must work in concert with cortical brain regions to store and recall memories. Findings that demonstrate the necessity of hippocampal-medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) communication in these processes, as well as findings that link the mPFC to memory storage, retrieval, and decision-making, have contributed to this growing area of study. Here, we review our current understanding of three questions related to this communication. What information is represented in the hippocampus and the mPFC? What are the underlying neural activity patterns and brain states that facilitate communication of those representations? What impact do these patterns have on the ability to learn and remember in new and familiar settings? We highlight evidence for bidirectional communication both during and after experience, and we discuss areas of active investigation to further uncover the role of bidirectional hippocampal-cortical interactions in the formation and maintenance of neural representations of memory.

item.title: Functional Network Organization Underlying Individual Differences in False Feedback Susceptibility: A Graph Theoretical Analysis.
item.description:
Human brain mapping
Individual differences in susceptibility to somatosensory false physiological feedback reflect variations in interoceptive processing, yet the underlying neural network mechanisms remain unclear. We analyzed resting-state functional connectivity using graph theoretical approaches in 41 healthy adults who completed a somatosensory false feedback paradigm. Nine regions of interest were defined from previous activation analyses, and network topology metrics including local efficiency, clustering coefficient, centrality measures, and path length were calculated across multiple thresholds. Three distinct patterns of network organization predicted false feedback susceptibility. Individuals more susceptible to false feedback showed: (1) increased posterior insula eccentricity, indicating network peripheralization of this key interoceptive region; (2) consistent orbitofrontal cortex segregation across multiple metrics including increased path length and decreased centrality measures; and (3) cerebellar network reconfiguration with reduced local efficiency but increased betweenness centrality. Somatosensory false feedback susceptibility reflects specific alterations in functional network topology, particularly reduced integration of interoceptive regions (posterior insula) and emotional appraisal systems (orbitofrontal cortex). These findings support a network-based model where interoceptive processing depends on efficient integration between visceral sensation, emotional evaluation, and cognitive control systems. Understanding these network properties may inform interventions targeting interoceptive awareness and emotional regulation.

item.title: Brain Regions Involved in Object-Location Memory in Healthy Adults: A Systematic Review and Activation Likelihood Estimation Meta-Analysis of Task-Based fMRI.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
The ability to remember where objects are located is a fundamental cognitive function particularly vulnerable to aging and neurodegenerative disease. Previous functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) research has combined object-location memory (OLM) with broader spatial-memory and -navigation tasks, resulting in inconsistent findings. This systematic review and coordinate-based activation likelihood estimation (ALE) meta-analysis isolated OLM to characterize brain regions engaged during encoding and retrieval in healthy adults, with additional exploratory analyses of age effects. Searches of PubMed, PsycInfo, and the Cochrane Library identified 21 eligible task-based fMRI studies comprising 622 participants. Twelve studies contributed to an encoding ALE, which identified significant spatial convergence in left and right ventral occipitotemporal regions encompassing the fusiform and parahippocampal gyri. The left cluster was supported by 8 of 12 experiments, survived all leave-one-experiment-out iterations, and was recovered by an independent coordinate-based framework, supporting a robust ventral occipitotemporal substrate for OLM encoding. An OLM retrieval ALE including four studies yielded no significant convergence, most likely reflecting the limited number of eligible studies. Retrieval findings were therefore synthesized narratively. These studies most frequently implicated the hippocampus and precuneus, suggesting a different regional pattern from encoding, although the phases were not statistically compared. Only three studies directly compared age groups, suggesting altered hippocampal engagement during retrieval in older adults. By isolating OLM from broader spatial-memory constructs, this review identifies a robust encoding substrate while highlighting current research gaps that need to be addressed. This review was preregistered on PROSPERO (CRD420251023695).

item.title: Distinct gradients of cortical architecture capture visual representations and behavior across the lifespan.
item.description:
eLife
The microstructure of cells within the human cerebral cortex varies across the cortical ribbon, where changes in cytoarchitecture and myeloarchitecture are thought to endow each region of the cortex with its unique function. While fine-scale relative to a cell, these changes at the population level impact architectural properties of the cortex measurable in vivo by noninvasive MRI, such as the thickness and myelin content of the cortex. This raises the question of whether or not we can use these in vivo architectural measures to understand cortical organization, function, and development more broadly. Using the human visual cortex as a test bed, we demonstrated two architectural gradients, one in which cytoarchitecture and myeloarchitecture converge and another in which they diverge. These two gradients underlie the structural and functional topography of the visual cortex, even predicting the presence of new visual representations. Moreover, the two gradients show distinct visual behavior relevance and lifespan trajectory. These findings provide a more general framework for understanding the human cortex, showing that architectural gradients are a measurable fingerprint of functional organization and ontogenetic routines in the human brain.

item.title: Interpretable embeddings of speech explain and enhance the brain encoding performance of audio models.
item.description:
PLoS computational biology
Speech foundation models (SFMs) are increasingly hailed as powerful computational models of human speech perception. However, since their representations are inherently black-box, it remains unclear what drives their alignment with brain responses. To remedy this, we built linear encoding models from six interpretable feature families: mel-spectrogram, Gabor filter bank features, speech presence, phonetic, syntactic, and semantic features, and contextualized embeddings from three state-of-the-art SFMs (Whisper, HuBERT, WavLM), quantifying electrocorticography (ECoG) response variance shared between feature classes. Variance-partitioning analyses revealed several key insights: First, the SFMs' alignment with the brain can be mostly accounted for by their ability to learn and encode simple interpretable speech features. Second, SFMs exhibit a systematic trade-off between encoding of brain-relevant low-level and high-level features across layers. Finally, our results show that SFMs learn brain-relevant semantics which cannot be accounted for by lower-level speech features, with this capacity increasing with model size and context length. Together, our findings suggest a principled approach to build more interpretable, accurate, and efficient encoding models of the brain by augmenting SFM embeddings with interpretable features.

item.title: Distinct roles of anterior cingulate and subcortical regions supporting effort evaluation versus preparation.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Cognitive effort encompasses the mental exertion invested to achieve a goal as well as the experienced cost associated with that exertion. The dopaminergic midbrain regions (i.e., ventral tegmental area/substantia nigra), ventral striatum, and anterior cingulate cortex have all been broadly implicated in effort regulation. However, less is known about the role of these regions in dissociable subprocesses such as effort evaluation versus effort preparation. In this preregistered functional MRI study with concurrent pupil tracking, we disentangled the evaluation and preparation phase of reward- and effort-based motivation. In the evaluation phase, the typical valuation regions encoded high-reward and low-effort demand as motivational factors. In the preparation phase, the anterior cingulate cortex displayed increased activity for demanding high-reward trials. The dopaminergic midbrain exhibited a positive reward effect only during task execution. The results suggest that when separating evaluation from preparation, regions traditionally thought of as primarily reward attuned respond to high reward and low effort during evaluation but can assign a motivating signal to effort during preparation, while the anterior cingulate cortex integrates effort and reward prospect to subserve only preparatory control processes.

item.title: Neural and cognitive correlates of adolescent anxiety: Widespread brain network alterations, increased control costs, and visuospatial processing deficits.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
This study investigated the neural substrates and cognitive correlates of adolescent anxiety, which are currently incompletely understood, in N = 3,499 youth with median (IQR) age 12.0 (1.1) years (~51.0% females), from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Study. Resting-state fMRI, structural MRI, anxiety (scores and related disorder diagnoses), and neurocognitive data were analyzed. Mixed-effects regression models were used to examine associations between anxiety, brain characteristics (topological and morphometric properties, and regulatory (control) costs of intrinsic network dynamics), and cognitive outcomes. Females, older youth, and those with more parental mental health problems had higher anxiety (β = 0.04-1.15, 95% CI = [0.01, 2.18]). Higher resting-state connectivity and/or centrality (network importance) of the cerebellum, amygdala, and thalamus, and higher cerebellum-basal-ganglia-thalamus control costs were associated with higher anxiety (β = 0.04-0.08, 95% CI = [0.01, 0.11]). In contrast, temporoparietal and frontoparietal network efficiency and resilience (robustness) were protective for social and/or generalized anxiety disorders (adjusted odds ratio (aOR) = 0.72-0.80, 95% CI = [0.62, 0.98]). Higher cortical thickness and/or volume of the superior temporal gyrus, pars opercularis, precentral gyrus, and putamen were associated with higher odds of generalized or social anxiety disorder (aOR = 1.28-1.44, 95% CI = [1.07, 1.78]). Finally, anxiety was associated with lower response accuracy in the Little Man Task (β = -0.05, 95% CI = [-0.09, -0.01]), and attenuated positive brain-task performance associations. These findings suggest that adolescent anxiety is associated with widespread brain alterations, especially in the cerebellum-basal ganglia-thalamus network, while the organization of frontoparietal and temporoparietal networks, which play as key role in emotion regulation and social function, is protective for anxiety disorders. It is also associated with lower visuospatial processing and alterations in the networks that support it.

item.title: Brain systems supporting the narrative self and psychopathology.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Disturbances in the narrative self are implicated across psychiatric disorders, with abnormalities in the neural systems supporting its generation and regulation constituting a transdiagnostic risk factor for mental illness. This review highlights how alterations in these brain systems underlie prevalent clinical features, including diminished, rigid, and sustained negative beliefs within the narrative self. The narrative self is framed as a higher-order construct that emerges from multiple systems, with reward, punishment, and motivational signals biasing which experiences are encoded as self-defining and which self-beliefs are reinforced over time. We discuss recent evidence demonstrating how the narrative self is supported by distributed brain networks in which subcortical inputs from the basal forebrain, habenula and mediodorsal thalamus modulate default mode network activity, with the salience, frontoparietal, cingulo-opercular, and hippocampal-parahippocampal networks regulating how self-beliefs are established or updated. Adolescence is emphasized as a developmental period uniquely vulnerable to disturbances in the formation of a coherent, flexible narrative self, wherein asynchronous subcortical and cortical development and pubertal changes interact to confer risk for diminished and rigid self-beliefs. Belief-updating tasks, hierarchical computational models, and ecological momentary assessment are proposed as approaches to quantify how self-beliefs form and shift across time, linking neural signatures of the narrative self to momentary variability. We propose that treating the narrative self as a primary level of explanation for psychopathology positions it as a testable target for future neuroimaging research, providing a clearer bridge from self-referential cognition to interventions in daily life.

item.title: Hexagonal modulation of theta rhythmic attentional sampling of visual space.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Spatial attention improves visual perception by selecting behaviorally relevant sensory signals. Traditionally, attention has been conceptualized as a static spotlight, while recent evidence posited that attention operates as a moving spotlight that samples visual space sequentially in discrete snapshots that are clocked by theta rhythms (∼3-8 Hz). While theta rhythmic attentional sampling has mainly been observed in fronto-parietal and occipital areas, theta oscillations also hallmark entorhinal-hippocampal grid-cell networks, which encode physical space in hexagonal patterns that guide overt exploration and navigation. We hypothesized that visual attention might rely on the same underlying principles and sample visual space in a hexagonal, grid-like configuration. To test this hypothesis, twenty participants (10 females and 10 males) performed a cue-guided attention task that probed behavioral performance as a function of space and time. Reaction times were assessed as a function of spatial location and varying cue-target intervals, which displayed spatially-structured theta rhythms. Specifically, higher theta power occurred at spatial locations that were aligned to multiples of 60°, consistent with an underlying hexagonal organization. Participants that exhibited stronger hexagonal sampling relied less on the spatial cue to guide their attentional allocation. In sum, these findings suggest that covert visual attention is organized in a hexagonal pattern that might be consistent with the grid-like structure known from the entorhinal-hippocampal system and highlight that theta rhythms could reflect a common organizing principle for spatial cognition.Significance Statement Attention prioritizes sensory inputs to optimize behavior. But how does attention sample the environment in space and time? Here, we demonstrate that attentional sampling of visual space is not uniform, but might preferentially explore locations that are oriented along a hexagonal pattern, reminiscent of the spatial configuration of entorhinal-hippocampal grid cells. Moreover, covert attentional sampling exhibited oscillatory theta signatures (3-8 Hz). In sum, these findings suggest that spatial attention and navigation may share a common organizing principle, and indicate that theta rhythms may orchestrate sampling behaviors in space and time as a unifying principle underlying spatial cognition.

item.title: Perception of tones versus tone streams under random multi-tone masking and its representation in auditory cortex.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
When repeated tones are presented among random masker tones, their perceptual organization is often variable. In some trials, they cannot be segregated from the masker tones. In other trials, often with a delay, they form coherent streams, segregated from the masker tones. A strong awareness-related negativity is evoked by each segregated tone of the stream in auditory cortex. A similar negative-going response has been observed when subtle, isolated tones are detected versus missed, raising the question of whether target tones that do not form a stream under informational masking are still perceived or not. Here a paradigm is introduced to probe this question while activity in auditory cortex was recorded with magnetoencephalography. Human listeners (13 female, 8 male) were instructed to indicate when they detected an isochronous stream of tones under multi-tone masking while listening to the stimulus. Thereafter, they indicated if a cue tone, presented subsequently to each trial, was comprised in the target and masker combination. Results confirmed that target tones could still be perceived in the subset of trials where they did not form a coherent stream, but the detectability in the cued frequency report was higher for tones forming a stream. A prominent awareness-related negativity was only observed when the tones formed a stream, suggesting that this response reflects the perceptual organization of the tones into streams and beyond the pure perception of the tones themselves. We speculate that the perceptual organization into a stream further enhances the detectability of the tones comprised in the stream.Significance Statement Tone sequences may form streams that segregate from competing aspects of the auditory scene, a phenomenon considered comparable to visual object grouping. In multi-tone masking, hearing out streams of repeated tones seemingly enhances tone detectability by a degree that makes it difficult to judge whether these tones could at all be perceived if they had not formed a coherent stream. We present a paradigm that allows for probing both, the perception of target-tone frequency and the formation of coherent streams in the same trials. Applying this setup in magnetoencephalography showed that the perceptual organization into a stream is more strongly represented in auditory cortex than the ability to correctly detect a tone frequency within a random tone masker.

item.title: Bivalent habenula modulation of human monoaminergic midbrain and cortical pathways.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
The habenula is implicated in signaling negative reward prediction errors (RPE), yet direct evidence demonstrating its influence on downstream human brain circuits is limited. Using ultra-high field (7T) fMRI and dynamic causal modelling across two negative RPE-inducing experimental tasks, we characterize habenula-directed connectivity with monoaminergic midbrain and cortical pathways in healthy adults (n = 47, 24 males and 23 females; n = 43, 23 males and 20 females). Negative feedback drove habenula inhibition of ventral tegmental area and dorsal raphe nucleus activity, while positive feedback had an excitatory effect. These core effects are replicated across reversal learning and perceptual decision uncertainty tasks, establishing a generalizable mechanism for behavioral adaptation. Task-specific modulatory effects emerged in pathways between the subcortical and cortical regions (ventral tegmental area→dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, dorsal raphe nucleus→medial prefrontal cortex, and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex→habenula), revealing context-dependent cortical elaboration of negative RPE-driven habenula signals. This provides the first evidence in humans, using model-based effective connectivity, for bivalent modulation of habenula function on monoaminergic midbrain and cortical pathways, demonstrating how the brain integrates negative and positive signals to guide adaptive behavior.Significance Statement The habenula - an epithalamic brain region - plays a key role in the encoding of reward and punishment. Animal studies have demonstrated the habenula to be bivalently modulated by aversive and appetitive stimuli, resulting in the bidirectional modulation of monoaminergic brain region activity. Despite this evidence, the directional impact of bivalently modulated habenula activity on its circuitry has yet to be investigated in humans. This study leverages ultra-high field (7T) fMRI and dynamic causal modelling to reveal the impact of bivalent habenula modulation on monoaminergic midbrain and cortical regions across two distinct tasks. Through these methodologies, we demonstrate the habenula to have a key role in guiding adaptive behavior.

item.title: The dual future of OPM-MEG: Clinical translation and naturalistic neuroscience.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Optically pumped magnetometer magnetoencephalography (OPM-MEG) has moved beyond proof of principle. The decisive question is no longer whether cryogen-free sensors can detect neuromagnetic fields from the human brain with sufficient sensitivity, but whether complete systems can deliver clinical decision value and interpretable recordings during more naturalistic behaviour. Here we argue that OPM-MEG is developing along two partly overlapping trajectories. One is clinical translation, where usefulness depends more on reliable workflows, calibrated source localisation, auditable quality control, and empirical evidence for improved diagnostic or treatment decisions. The other is naturalistic neuroscience, where wearable measurement can connect neural dynamics to movement, action, and social behaviour without conflating neural activity with movement-related artefacts. Both trajectories depend on a shared engineering stack including magnetic field control, dense spatial sampling, accurate calibration, integrated electronics, artefact suppression, participant comfort, and synchronised behavioural measurement. The next stage of OPM-MEG should be evaluated by clinical utility in specific patient groups, statistically identifiable neural dynamics in behaviourally rich settings, and sufficient system detail for replication across systems and sites.

item.title: Attention selectively enhances collision sensitivity in the superficial SC, PBGN and centromedial amygdala to looming stimuli in the upper visual field.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Accurate detection of impending collisions is essential for survival. While multiple subcortical pathways have been implicated in the detection of looming stimuli, the roles of top-down attention and conscious awareness in this process remain unclear. Using high-resolution fMRI, we investigated how top-down attention and conscious awareness influence subcortical processing of approaching objects on collision versus near-miss trajectories. In healthy participants, the superficial layers of the superior colliculus (SCs), the parabigeminal nucleus (PBGN), and the centromedial amygdala (CMA) exhibited significantly stronger activation to hit-nasion than to near-miss trajectories in the upper visual field, but only when participants attended to the approaching object. Correlation and path analysis of collision sensitivity and beta-series functional connectivity consistently revealed a significant SC-PBGN connection. For stimuli presented in the blind visual field of hemianopic patients, significant functional connectivity was observed between the SC and both the pulvinar and the ventral tegmental area (VTA) in response to collision trajectories. Together, these findings suggest that attention selectively enhances collision sensitivity in the SCs-PBGN-CMA pathway for accurate detection of collision trajectory in the upper visual field, whereas the SC-pulvinar and SC-VTA pathways are associated with collision detection in the absence of conscious awareness.

item.title: Cerebellar subregions support social cognition in early behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Social cognitive deficits manifest early in behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD), compromising individuals' ability to interpret social cues, empathize, and maintain interpersonal relationships. Current neurobiological models emphasize cortical network disruption, particularly within the salience, semantic appraisal, and default mode networks, as primary contributors to social dysfunction. However, despite the increasingly recognized role of the cerebellum in higher-order cognitive and socioemotional processes, its contributions to social deficits remains underexplored in bvFTD. Here, we investigated the unique and network-level influences of cerebellar subregions on social cognition across experimental and real-world assessments in early-stage bvFTD. A total of 107 individuals with bvFTD and 100 healthy controls were evaluated across three social domains: theory of mind (ToM) (The Awareness of Social Inference Test-Social Inference-Enriched, TASIT-SIE; Cognitive Emotional Perspective Taking Test), emotion reading (Dynamic Affect Recognition Test; TASIT-Emotion Evaluation Test; Comprehensive Affect Testing System), and real-life empathy (Revised Self-Monitoring Scale; Interpersonal Reactivity Index). Using a functional cerebellar parcellation, we extracted volumes of posterior cerebellar subregions implicated in social-linguistic and multiple-demand networks from participants' structural MRIs. To address the high collinearity between cerebellar and cortical atrophy patterns, we applied sequential regression, partial least squares correlation, and dominance analysis to characterize brain-behavior relationships. Additionally, supplementary structural equation modelling (SEM) examined whether the associations between cerebellar integrity and social cognition was mediated by executive functioning. Our results showed that cerebellar subregional integrity contributed to social cognitive deficits in individuals with early-stage bvFTD. Cerebellar subregions, particularly right Crus I and II, showed the strongest and most selective contribution to high-level inferential Theory of Mind performance. Tasks involving dynamic emotion stimuli exhibited a more distributed pattern of cerebello-cerebral involvement. By contrast, questionnaire-based measures of real-world social functioning were less prominently represented in the latent covariance structure. SEM further showed that cerebellar integrity remained directly associated with social cognition after accounting for executive functioning, whereas the indirect association through executive functioning was not significant. These findings highlight the task-dependent nature of cerebellar involvement in social cognition, and demonstrate that time-limited experimental tasks, particularly those involving inferential reasoning about beliefs and affect, are likely to be especially valuable in detecting subtle cerebello-cerebral network dysfunction that questionnaire-based measures may overlook. Our results extend cortex-centric models of social dysfunction in bvFTD by demonstrating that cerebellar subregions contribute to distributed cerebello-cerebral systems associated with social cognitive performance. These findings provide a foundation for future longitudinal and mechanistic studies of cerebello-cerebral dysfunction in neurodegenerative disease.

item.title: Peripersonal space: a neural system mapping self-environment interaction 'here and now'.
item.description:
Trends in cognitive sciences
The space surrounding the body where physical interactions with external stimuli occur is referred to as peripersonal space (PPS). Traditionally conceived as a spatial construct, PPS is better understood as a neural representation that integrates bodily inputs with external cues to predict body-object interactions. After summarizing its multisensory, motor, and plastic properties, this review draws on computational models to examine how PPS captures statistical regularities of body-object interactions. This predictive function may position PPS as an interface between self and environment, contributing to minimal self-consciousness and its alterations across states of consciousness and neuropsychiatric conditions. Recent findings extend this framework to the inner body, suggesting that interoceptive signals shape PPS and that PPS-related processing may influence immune responses.

item.title: Does Phubbing Always Elicit Social Pain? The Role of Belonging Context.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Phubbing, a prevalent interpersonal phenomenon in which individuals divert their attention to their phones while neglecting their interaction partners during face-to-face interactions, has been associated with adverse psychological and relational outcomes, including social pain. However, the same "eyes-on-phone" behavior may not always be experienced as phubbing or evoke feelings of neglect and social pain. The present research examined whether belonging context shapes behavioral and neural responses to "eyes-on-phone" behavior during face-to-face interaction. In Study 1, 163 participants completed a scenario-based task that required them to judge how they felt about several stories, in which belonging context (positive, negative, unrelated) was crossed with attentional state (eyes-on-phone, eyes-on-you). In Study 2, 50 participants completed the Cyberball paradigm to manipulate different belonging contexts (positive, negative, unrelated) with 6 models, followed by an ERP experiment in which they judged whether images of these models displaying different attentional states (eyes-on-phone, eyes-on-you) made them feel neglect-related social pain. Across both studies, within "positive" contexts, "eyes-on-phone" behavior elicited greater social pain, including perceived neglect, emotional unpleasantness, and unwillingness to communicate (Study 1), as well as a greater tendency to endorse neglect-related social pain and larger P3 amplitudes (Study 2) than "eyes-on-you" behavior, whereas this pattern was not consistently observed in the "negative" or "unrelated" contexts. These findings indicate that phubbing is not inherently experienced as social pain. Rather, its social meaning depends on prior belonging context: a mismatch between contextual cues and subsequent attentional behavior may give rise to expectancy violations, which could contribute to social pain when the behavior is interpreted as neglectful.
